newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communists mark Revolution amid Soviet nostalgia.
newsitem.headline: Communists mark Revolution amid Soviet nostalgia.

text.p: Russia's communists, still struggling to digest their fall from power five years ago, rallied in central Moscow on Thursday to mark the 79th anniversary of Lenin's seizure of power.
They took to the streets as President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from heart bypass surgery, signed a decree to rename the holiday the Day of Accord and Reconciliation.
The huge parades on Red Square for what was the main annual Soviet holiday are gone but the rally allowed demonstrators to wallow in nostalgia for the good old days.
They began with the old Soviet anthem blasting from loudspeakers and ended with the Marxist anthem The Internationale.
Speakers standing on a truck parked in front of the statue of Karl Marx opposite the Bolshoi Theatre denounced President Boris Yeltsin's "sell-out regime" for restoring capitalism.
There was special venom against "the red-haired cardinal" Anatoly Chubais, now Yeltsin's chief of staff and previously the architect of privatisation.
"Chubais to prison!" yelled Viktor Anpilov, leader of the hardline Working Moscow communist group, who called for a "March on Moscow" to overthrow Yeltsin's regime.
Yeltsin, recovering from bypass surgery, signed a decree as the rally got under way to rename the day. He said he wanted to avoid confrontation and acted "in the interests of unity".

Gennady Zyuganov, leader of the mainstream Communist Party of the Russian Federation, sounded a more moderate note than the radicals, stressing that his party opposed violence and sought power only by legal means.
Zyuganov accused Yeltsin of turning his operation into a "show" by handing over his powers for a day to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

"This spectacle of a one-day president for 23 hours has made us a laughingstock in the eyes of the world community," said Zyuganov, who lost to Yeltsin in the second round of this year's presidential election.

A crowd of several thousand, mostly elderly, people marched to the rally in unseasonably warm weather, trudging with their red banners past the luxury hotels and shops which have sprung up in the centre of the capital since 1991.
Zyuganov has tried to lead his party, many of whose supporters are pensioners, towards a more nationalist course, playing down the Soviet legacy in favour of Russian patriotism.
But it was clear the vast majority of the crowd wanted a simple promise of a return to the Soviet past, and chanted "Soviet Union, Soviet Union".
Many of the demonstrators carried portraits of dictator Josef Stalin and slogans denouncing Chubais and Yeltsin.

One called for the sacking of "cosmopolitans with dual citizenship" -- a reference to the recent appointment as deputy secretary of Russia's Security Council of controversial Jewish businessman Boris Berezovsky. Newspaper reports have said he has dual Russian and Israeli citizenship.

Though Anpilov and Zyuganov shared the platform and there were calls for unity, there was no disguising the splits between the mainstream heirs of the Soviet party and the radical hardliners from Anpilov's movement and the Russian Communist Workers Party.

Zyuganov's communist faction in parliament voted to confirm the government of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in office in August but has reaped nothing concrete in return. It is now calling for a "government of national interest".
The anniversary of the Bolshevik coup d'etat in St Petersburg in 1917 was the main annual holiday in Soviet times. Its leaders traditionally took the salute at a military parade on Red Square.

Such parades and demonstrations are now forbidden on Red Square and 1917 is officially regarded as a disaster for Russia, but Yeltsin's government has reluctantly bowed to the popular mood by retaining November 7 as a holiday.
A poll published on Wednesday by Interfax news agency said 46 per cent of Russians believe the revolution played a positive role, 33 per cent disagreed and the remainder had no opinion.

One speaker warned that the Russian people were threatened with extinction but were beginning to resist. "The Russian bear has come out of his cave growling but he needs the blindfold to be pulled from his eyes," he said.
